issues.legal_issue: An inquiry under Rule 4 of the Land Acquisition (Companies) Rules, 1963 need not be completed before a preliminary acquisition notification is issued for land intended for a company.
material_facts: A company applied for acquisition of land for a company purpose.
The government issued the preliminary acquisition notification before giving notice of the Rule 4 inquiry.
The landowner objected to the preliminary notification, and the government later conducted the statutory objections inquiry and the Rule 4 inquiry.
The government executed an agreement with the company and then issued the final acquisition declaration.
The High Court quashed both notifications solely because the Rule 4 inquiry had not preceded the preliminary notification.
issues.conclusion: The Rule 4 inquiry is not a mandatory prerequisite to issuing the preliminary notification; it must, however, precede the final declaration. The High Court’s ruling on this ground was set aside.
issues.legal_principle: Under the scheme of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 and the Land Acquisition (Companies) Rules, 1963, the preliminary notification may issue when it appears to the government that the land is needed for a public purpose or a company; the government’s satisfaction and the Rule 4 inquiry are required before the final declaration. Rule 4(4) conditions the declaration on consultation with the committee, consideration of the Rule 4 report and any report under section 5A, and execution of the section 41 agreement. The Court followed Babu Barkya Thakur v. State of Bombay, approved Raja Ram Jaiswal v. Collector, Allahabad, distinguished Abdul Husein Tayabali v. State of Gujarat, and treated the contrary observation in General Govt. Servants Co-operative Housing Society Ltd. v. Wahab Uddin as inadvertent and, in any event, obiter. The preliminary notification also fixes the date relevant to market-value compensation under section 23.

predicates.company_land_acquisition: The government initiated acquisition proceedings for land sought by a company.
predicates.appeal_from_quashing_acquisition_notific: An appeal challenged a decision that had quashed acquisition notifications.
predicates.rule_inquiry_followed_preliminary_notifi: The government conducted the company-acquisition inquiry after issuing the preliminary notification.

issues.definition: When an appeal concerns company land-acquisition notifications and the inquiry followed the preliminary notification, the preliminary notification is not invalid solely because the inquiry came later.

issues.legal_issue: A court deciding a matter that raises several factual and legal grounds should address all of them rather than dispose of the matter on only one ground when further appeal is available.
material_facts: The landowner challenged the acquisition notifications on several factual and legal grounds.
The High Court quashed the notifications on the Rule 4 timing ground and did not decide the other grounds.
The appeal succeeded on the timing ground, leaving the other challenges unresolved.
issues.conclusion: The Court set aside the High Court’s decision on the timing ground and remitted the matter for the High Court to decide the remaining grounds.
issues.legal_principle: To avoid delay and protraction of litigation, a court should, where an appeal is available, dispose of all the points raised rather than rest its decision on a single point. The Court relied on an observation of the Privy Council, whose case is not identified in the supplied judgment.

predicates.appeal_from_lower_court_decision: A party appealed from a lower court’s decision in a matter where further appeal was available.
predicates.multiple_factual_or_legal_grounds: The case presented more than one factual or legal ground for decision.
predicates.lower_court_decided_only_one_ground: The lower court decided one ground and left the other grounds unresolved.

issues.definition: When an appeal follows a decision that resolved only one of several grounds, the unresolved grounds are remitted for decision.
